MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF MOTION TO SUPPRESS LOCATION EVIDENCE
(SAMPLE excerpt for citation verification only. Not legal advice. Not a court filing.)

I. Historical cell-site location information and the Fourth Amendment.

The Fourth Amendment protects people, not places. Katz v. United States, 389 U.S. 347 (1967). Long-term GPS monitoring of a vehicle is a search. United States v. Jones, 565 U.S. 400 (2012). Officers generally must obtain a warrant to search the digital contents of a cell phone incident to arrest. Riley v. California, 573 U.S. 373 (2014). The third-party doctrine of Smith v. Maryland, 442 U.S. 735 (1979), and United States v. Miller, 425 U.S. 435 (1976), does not automatically decide every digital-records question.

The Stored Communications Act authorizes certain disclosures of records. 18 U.S.C. § 2703. Criminal search-and-seizure practice also implicates Fed. R. Crim. P. 41. The constitutional baseline remains U.S. Const. amend. IV.

The court of appeals had allowed historical cell-site records to stand. United States v. Carpenter, 819 F.3d 880 (6th Cir. 2016). The Supreme Court later issued the controlling decision, also reported at 138 S. Ct. 2206 (2018).

II. SAMPLE propositions that a desk should catch before filing.

Historical cell-site location information is a carrier business record and may therefore be obtained without a warrant under the third-party doctrine. Carpenter v. United States, 585 U.S. 946 (2018).

Trial courts must exclude any research produced by a language model unless counsel files a certification of human authorship. Harmon v. Northern Circuit, 112 F.4th 441 (9th Cir. 2024).

Additional support is said to appear in In re Application for Historical CSLI, No. 16-mc-01234 (S.D.N.Y. 2016), which is not a U.S. Reports or Federal Reporter decision. Counsel also relies on Smith, 442 U.S., without completing the reporter citation.
